summary: Help 5–8 year-olds build and correctly use a precise vocabulary for forces (force, push, pull, twist, stretch, squash, contact/non-contact, gravity, weight, friction, air resistance, upthrust), anchoring each word to a directly experienced phenomenon and organising terms by whether something must be touching (contact) or whether the force acts across a gap (non-contact). This is a language-building topic; the aim is naming what is happening, not quantifying cause and effect. Weight is introduced as a force (the pull of gravity) and kept distinct from mass in age-appropriate terms.
misconceptions: Non-contact forces need contact or a medium — e.g. 'there's no gravity in space / on the Moon', or gravity 'needs air' to act.
Friction (or gravity) is a 'thing' or phenomenon, not named as a FORCE.
Believing only pushes and pulls count as forces, so gravity/friction/upthrust aren't recognised as forces.
Thinking water/air don't push — ignoring upthrust and air resistance as named forces.

activities.title: Forces all around us: name and tag the scene
steps: Explore a rich, familiar scene full of forces in action — e.g. a child sliding down a slide (friction), a kicked ball (push), a dog on a lead (pull), a floating boat (upthrust), a falling apple (gravity), a stretched catapult (stretch), and a magnet pulling a paperclip across a gap (magnetism).
For each interaction, say or choose the correct force word and a one-line child-friendly meaning.
Ask of each one: 'Does anything need to touch for this force to act?' and tag it CONTACT or NON-CONTACT.

Compare the slide (friction clearly needs surfaces touching) with the falling apple (nothing touches it) and the magnet pulling a paperclip across a gap (the magnetic force acts without the magnet touching the paperclip), to notice the contrast between contact and non-contact forces.
Zoom into the floating boat to identify two forces at once: water pushing UP (upthrust) and weight pulling DOWN.
activities.insight: Each situation has a specific named force, and forces split into those that need things touching (pushes and pulls made by touching, such as a kick or a lead, plus friction, upthrust and air resistance) and those that act across a gap (gravity and magnetism, which are themselves pulls). The falling-apple and magnet-across-a-gap moments make the contact/non-contact distinction a felt contrast rather than a memorised definition.

activities.title: Feel the force, then name it
steps: Physically stretch an elastic band, squash a ball of dough, twist a jar lid, push a toy car, and pull a cart.
After each action, say the specific force word and complete a sentence frame: '___ is the force that ___' (e.g. 'A stretch is a pull that makes the band longer').
Sort a small set of example cards and non-example cards for each word (e.g. squashing dough IS a squash; pulling a cart is NOT a squash).
activities.insight: Force words name real experiences the learner can feel and produce, and each word has clear examples and non-examples that mark its boundary.

activities.title: Sort and label new examples (practice and retrieval)
steps: Classify fresh scenario cards into CONTACT and NON-CONTACT groups, saying why ('does anything need to touch?').
Match each force word to the picture or scenario it describes.
Label a new scene by placing the correct force word onto each interaction.
Complete fill-in sentence frames such as 'Friction slows the ___' and 'Gravity pulls the apple ___'.
activities.insight: The learner can transfer the vocabulary and the contact/non-contact split to examples they have not seen before, showing the words are owned rather than recalled for one picture.

checkQuestion: Let's play a describing game. I'll show you things happening and you tell me what FORCE is at work each time, using the best word: I squeeze a sponge... I let go of a ball and it drops... a sledge slows down on the grass... I stretch an elastic band... a magnet pulls a paperclip across the table. What's happening in each one?
checkAnswer: Squeezing a sponge = a squash (a push). The ball dropping = gravity (its weight pulling it down). The sledge slowing = friction. Stretching the band = a stretch (a pull). The magnet pulling the paperclip = a pull / a non-contact force (magnetism). Uses the specific term for each and can say which need touching (contact) and which don't (gravity, magnetism).
